title: Dicey's Formulation of the Rule of Law

content.overview: A.V. Dicey's classical formulation of the rule of law emphasised supremacy of law over arbitrary power, equality before the ordinary courts, and the constitution as the result of ordinary law. Modern administrative law both draws on and revises Dicey's account in light of the welfare state and written constitutions.
content.glance: State Dicey's three limbs; note modern criticisms (discretion, administrative tribunals, written constitutions); and apply the enduring core — non-arbitrariness and equality — to the problem.
content.study: Dicey associated the rule of law with (1) absence of arbitrary power, (2) equality before the ordinary law administered by ordinary courts, and (3) the constitution as the product of ordinary law protecting individual rights. Twentieth-century developments — wide administrative discretion, specialised tribunals and written constitutions with judicial review — have required adaptation. The enduring core is that public power must be authorised by law and exercised without arbitrariness. Indian constitutionalism absorbs the core while rejecting Dicey's hostility to administrative law as such. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the Constitution. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of this doctrine.

sections.heading: Dicey's Three Limbs
sections.body: Supremacy of law; equality before ordinary courts; constitution as result of ordinary law.

sections.heading: Historical Context
sections.body: Dicey wrote against continental droit administratif and wide prerogative discretion.

sections.heading: Modern Critiques
sections.body: Welfare-state discretion, tribunals and written constitutions challenge strict Diceyan assumptions.

sections.heading: Enduring Core
sections.body: Non-arbitrariness and legal authorisation of power remain central.

sections.heading: Indian Reception
sections.body: Indian constitutionalism absorbs the core while rejecting Dicey's hostility to administrative law as such.

examples.title: Arbitrary discretion
examples.body: An authority exercises a power without any legal standard or relevant consideration. Dicey's first limb and Article 14 non-arbitrariness both condemn the action.

examples.title: Tribunal versus ordinary court
examples.body: A statute channels disputes to a specialised tribunal. Modern admin law accepts this departure from strict Diceyan equality before ordinary courts, subject to independence and judicial review.

hypotheticals.question: Did Dicey deny all administrative discretion?
hypotheticals.analysis: He opposed arbitrary discretionary power, not all authorised discretion.

hypotheticals.question: Is Dicey binding Indian precedent?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. He is a classical theorist; Indian law is governed by the Constitution and statutes.

distinctions.title: Diceyan rule of law vs constitutional rule of law in India
distinctions.left: Ordinary law and ordinary courts emphasis
distinctions.right: Written Constitution, basic structure and judicial review

misconceptions.correction: He opposed arbitrary discretionary power, not all authorised discretion.

misconceptions.trap: Dicey is directly binding Indian precedent.
misconceptions.correction: He is a classical theorist; Indian law is governed by the Constitution and statutes.

cases.name: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
cases.facts: Constitutional amendments and the extent of Parliament's amending power.
cases.issue: What constitutional limitations govern amendment power?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Constitution has a basic structure that cannot be destroyed by amendment.
cases.relevance: Authority already in the file on constitutional supremacy and rule of law.

cases.name: I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu
cases.facts: Ninth Schedule immunity against judicial review.
cases.issue: Whether constitutional insulation from review is unlimited.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Post-Kesavananda Ninth Schedule laws remain reviewable on basic-structure grounds.

cases.name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain
cases.issue: Whether essential constitutional principles may be displaced by amendment.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Rule of law, democracy and judicial review are integral to the constitutional structure.
cases.holding: Impugned provisions invalid to the extent they damaged basic constitutional principles.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Dicey problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. State three limbs. II. Note modern critiques. III. Apply non-arbitrariness core. IV. Link to Indian constitutional standards.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: State Dicey's limbs; distinguish theory from Indian positive law; apply Article 14 and judicial review.
